extracted.intended_audience: OSHA stakeholders, regulated employers, public commenters, policymakers, and occupational health/economic analysts reviewing the proposed heat standard
extracted.subtask_short: estimating benefits for OSHA heat standard
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and data standards OSHA uses to estimate fatalities, non-fatal heat-related injuries and illnesses (HRIs), and the quantifiable benefits of the proposed Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard, including adjustments for underreporting and sensitivity/uncertainty analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary data sources for fatalities and HRIs
rubrics_metrics.description: The IIF program collects data annually through two major surveys: the Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries (CFOI) and the Survey of Occupational Injuries and Illnesses (SOII). OSHA used data from the BLS IIF program for its analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CFOI for occupational fatalities and SOII for non-fatal injuries and illnesses as the primary authoritative datasets when estimating workplace heat-related outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of heat-related incidents using BLS event code 531
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA identified the number of heat-related fatalities and HRIs by searching BLS' CFOI and SOII databases for incidents captured under BLS event or exposure classification code 531—Exposure to Environmental Heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict counts to incidents classified under event/exposure code 531 to maintain consistency with BLS categorizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: OSHA four-step method to estimate industry fatalities with undisclosed data
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA used four steps to estimate the number of industry fatalities in years with undisclosed BLS data: (1) compare total annual fatalities to sum of private industry and government, and assign the difference to the undisclosed category; (2) compare private industry total to sum of goods-producing and service-providing, and if undisclosed use historical proportioning; (3) for underlying super-sectors, distribute differences across undisclosed super-sectors proportional to non-fatal HRI distribution; (4) for government, compute residuals and evenly distribute across undisclosed government ownerships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When BLS suppresses industry/detail cells, (a) set undisclosed category = total minus known published counts; (b) use historical average shares to split private industry into goods vs services when current-year data are undisclosed; (c) allocate residuals among undisclosed super-sectors using their share of non-fatal HRIs; (d) for government ownership types, evenly distribute residuals across the ownership types with undisclosed estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical average share (63%/37%) to allocate private industry fatalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the data from 2011-2018, OSHA divided the average percentage of heat-related private industry fatalities that were attributable to each group, estimating that 63 percent of private industry fatalities were in goods-producing industries and the remaining 37 percent were in service-producing industries. OSHA applied these percentages in years with undisclosed data (2019-2022).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When current-year goods vs service private-industry splits are undisclosed, multiply total private-industry fatalities by the historical average shares (63% goods-producing, 37% service-providing) to estimate the split.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribute undisclosed super-sector fatalities proportional to non-fatal HRI shares
rubrics_metrics.description: For years where the comparison showed a mismatch due to undisclosed data, OSHA estimated the data for the undisclosed super-sectors by distributing the difference between the total annual fatalities and the sum of fatalities in the underlying super-sectors across the super-sectors with undisclosed data. The estimate for these undisclosed super-sectors was set equal to the difference described above multiplied by the percentage of non-fatal heat-related incidents by super-sector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the super-sector's share of non-fatal HRIs (estimated average annual non-fatal incidents) as weights to apportion residual/fill-in values for suppressed fatality counts at the super-sector level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even distribution of residual government fatalities across undisclosed ownership types
rubrics_metrics.description: For each year, OSHA calculated the difference between the total annual heat-related fatalities in government and the sum of annual fatality counts by all government ownership types (Federal, State, and local). OSHA assumed this difference represents the number of fatalities for ownership types with undisclosed yearly estimates. OSHA evenly distributed the difference across all government ownerships with undisclosed estimates for that year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When government ownership-level fatality cells are suppressed, allocate the residual equally across the undisclosed ownership-type cells (e.g., if total government residual = 4 and three ownership types undisclosed, assign 4/3 to each).

rubrics_metrics.name: Present underreporting-adjusted counts and discuss underreporting uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a discussion of underreporting issues surrounding these data which leads to a presentation of OSHA's underreporting adjusted count of HRIs and heat-related fatalities. Even with this adjustment, there remains a great deal of uncertainty surrounding the extent of underreporting, other parameters used in this estimation of health and safety benefits, as well as additional potential benefits, all of which the agency discusses next in an uncertainty analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust raw BLS counts for underreporting but explicitly present and discuss the uncertainty around the magnitude of underreporting and how it affects benefit estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize four causes of underreporting
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA has determined that heat-related occupational fatalities and HRIs are underreported due to (1) employers not being fully compliant with recordkeeping rules, (2) employees not reporting cases to their employers, (3) a lack of identifying heat as the cause of a heat-related injury or illness, and (4) the scope and inclusion criteria of the various surveillance data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing data completeness, consider these four specific mechanisms that bias BLS/administrative counts downward and discuss their implications for adjusted estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: CFOI considered authoritative but may misclassify heat-specific causes
rubrics_metrics.description: BLS CFOI is well-regarded as the most complete and authoritative source on fatal workplace injuries and estimates of its magnitude of underreporting of occupational fatalities do not exist. However, there may be factors specific to heat-related fatalities that make CFOI particularly likely to misclassify the cause of death as being due to some other cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat CFOI counts as authoritative baseline data but document potential heat-specific misclassification risk and incorporate that uncertainty into estimates or sensitivity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use SOII days-away-from-work categories and median days metric
rubrics_metrics.description: From 2011 to 2022, SOII recorded a total of 39,450 HRIs that required days away from work. As detailed, 35.8% required one day away, 21.5% required two days, 23.9% needed three to five days, and the remaining required six or more days. Median days away from work is 2 and is used to summarize varying lengths of absence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report distribution across standard days-away-from-work categories and summarize absence severity using median days away as the summary statistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report incidence rates per 100,000 full-time workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Table VIII.E.4. details the BLS' SOII estimates of annual incidence rates of HRIs between 2011 and 2022. Over this period, the average estimated annual incidence rate is 3 cases per 100,000 full-time workers for HRIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express non-fatal HRI frequency as incidence rates per 100,000 full-time workers (and report year-by-year rates and multi-year averages) for comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for SOII population/scope exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The SOII excludes all work-related fatalities as well as non-fatal work injuries and illnesses to the self-employed, to workers on farms with 10 or fewer employees, to private household workers; to volunteers, and to Federal Government workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting SOII-based counts, explicitly note the excluded worker populations and consider whether to adjust or qualitatively discuss omitted groups in benefit estimation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensitivity analysis to show range of potential quantifiable benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: This section includes a sensitivity analysis that calculates the potential benefits of this standard assuming different parameters to demonstrate the range of potential quantifiable benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run alternative parameterizations (e.g., varying underreporting multipliers, incidence assumptions, industry allocations) and present sensitivity results to illustrate uncertainty in benefit estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat BLS biennial estimates appropriately starting 2021
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting with 2021, BLS published data biennially. The number of HRIs reported for 2021 and 2022 is a biennial estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using post-2020 SOII data, account for biennial reporting (2021 & 2022 combined estimate) rather than annual estimates and adjust trend analyses accordingly.
